ROB 498 / 599 · Fall 2026

3D Robot Perception

How a robot builds, maintains, and acts on a model of the 3D world it can only ever see partially, noisily, and from wherever it happens to be standing.

Instructor Bernadette Bucher Meets MW · 1303 EECS Term Aug 31 – Dec 9 Guest lectures Four CV prerequisite None

01 · About

An advanced, paper-driven course on spatial perception for robots

Robots act in a 3D world they observe through imperfect sensors, from a moving body, under a deadline. This course covers how a robot represents that world and keeps the representation useful: how 3D geometry is reconstructed from real sensor data, how semantics and object-level structure are attached to it, how that structure is compressed into scene graphs and spatial memory a planner or language model can query, and how learned world models predict what happens next under the robot's own actions.

The course is topical. Roughly half the reading list postdates 2024, and four guest lectures bring in researchers who wrote the work being covered. You will build a working 3D perception stack across three labs and carry a team research project from proposal to demonstration.

By the end of the course you can

  • Choose a 3D representation from the downstream task, collision checking, grasp synthesis, navigation, rendering, and justify the memory, latency, and accuracy tradeoff.
  • Compose and calibrate a multi-sensor 3D perception stack, and reason about pose and its uncertainty on SE(3).
  • Build a metric-semantic map and a queryable 3D scene graph from a posed RGB-D sequence using open-vocabulary 2D foundation models.
  • Explain what a world model predicts, what it is conditioned on, and why visual fidelity is a poor proxy for usefulness in closed-loop control.
  • Read, present, and critique a current research paper, and reproduce a published result well enough to know where it breaks.

03 · Prerequisites

What you need before Week 1

  • Programming: EECS 281 or equivalent. Fluency in Python is assumed and not taught.
  • Math: working knowledge of linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability. Eigendecomposition, SVD, least squares, and nonlinear optimization are reviewed as needed.
  • Deep learning: familiarity with autograd, CNNs, and transformer basics is helpful and not required, L05 covers what the course uses.
  • Computer vision: not required and not assumed.

The crash course, taught in class, Weeks 1–3

Everything this course needs from classical computer vision and deep learning is taught in the first five lectures, not assigned as homework. This is a change from previous years, when the same material was two asynchronous modules: Lab 1 depends on it, and reading it alone is where people fell behind without noticing.

A · Geometric vision, L01, L03, L04. Pinhole camera and calibration, epipolar geometry, stereo matching and the depth-error law, features and descriptors, RANSAC, triangulation, PnP, bundle adjustment.

B · Deep learning, L05. Autograd and backpropagation, CNNs and why 3D breaks them, attention and permutation equivariance, training practicalities.

The written module notes remain the reference. They carry the full derivations, the Used by and Trap boxes, and the self-checks, and they are the right place to go when a lecture moves faster than you want. The diagnostic is two Canvas quizzes, each covering only what has already been lectured. Quiz 1 (geometry and estimation, L01–L03) is due Sunday Sep 13; quiz 2 (sensing and learning, L04–L05) is due Sunday Sep 20. Open notes, unlimited attempts, and both stay retakeable to full credit through Sunday Sep 27, highest score kept. They exist to tell you what to reread, not to sort you: the feedback names the topics you missed.

If you have taken EECS 442, CMU 16-385, or an equivalent, much of L01 and L03 will be revision; the module page carries a topic-by-topic mapping so you can see what is new. The parts that are new to almost everyone are the depth-error law in L04, the observability arguments, and the memory arithmetic in L05.

Curriculum

Five units, twenty-three lectures

Each unit assumes the representations built in the one before it.

UNIT 0

Foundations for embodied 3D

Weeks 1–3 · 5 lectures

What makes robot perception different from computer vision: a camera you control is a different problem from a dataset you are handed, and the toolkit the rest of the course runs on: rigid-body state, the geometry that turns a 3D world into pixels and back, sensor physics, and what a learned function can add to any of it. The classical-vision and deep-learning background is taught here, in class, across these five meetings; the bridge module notes remain the written reference and carry the self-checks.

  • L01What embodiment changesCourse information and logistics. Then: closed-loop versus open-loop perception, latency, partial observability, metric scale, and the asymmetric cost of being wrong. Perception as an action: a robot produces its dataset rather than receiving it. Then the crash course opens: the pinhole camera, homogeneous coordinates, intrinsics and extrinsics, the camera matrix and its eleven degrees of freedom, distortion, and calibration as an estimation problem.Slides →annotated PDFwrite-in PDF
  • L02Rigid-body geometry and stateSO(3) and SE(3) as groups rather than as matrices. The Lie algebra, the exponential and log maps, and where the small-angle form loses all its precision. Uncertainty as a tangent-space covariance, the adjoint, and the lever arm that turns base rotation error into sensor position error. Frames, transform trees, and extrinsics as parameters you estimate. PnP posed as relocalisation, optimised on the manifold.Slides →annotated PDFwrite-in PDF
  • L03Two views, correspondence, and robust estimationEpipolar geometry, the essential and fundamental matrices, and the normalised eight-point algorithm. What makes a point matchable: the second-moment matrix, scale, descriptors, and their learned replacements. RANSAC, its iteration count, and why the minimal sample size sits in an exponent. Triangulation, bundle adjustment, and the factor graph the whole back end is built on.Slides · Wed Sep 9
  • L043D sensing physicsStereo, structured light, time of flight, spinning and solid-state LiDAR, event cameras, radar. Passive versus active sensing, and what a sensor that emits gets in return. The Z² depth-error law and what it means for how you weight a fusion. Motion distortion and de-skewing, flying pixels, extrinsic calibration and its observability conditions, and time synchronisation.Slides · Mon Sep 14
  • L05The learning half of the crash courseAutograd as a graph computation, why reverse mode is the right choice, and why activations rather than parameters fill your GPU. Convolution as a set of assumptions about a grid, and the memory arithmetic that rules out dense 3D convolution. Sparsity, sparse and submanifold convolution. Point clouds as sets: permutation invariance, PointNet, and why attention fitted 3D without being adapted to it. Training practicalities, evaluation traps, and the reproducibility the labs grade.Slides · Wed Sep 16
UNIT 1

Representing and reconstructing 3D

Weeks 4–6 · 5 lectures

The representation catalog, then the two reconstruction paradigms currently competing: per-scene optimization and feed-forward inference. Running through both is the question of which measurement to take next.

  • L06The representation catalog, and learning on itPoint clouds, voxels and octrees, TSDF and ESDF, meshes, implicit SDF and occupancy, 3D Gaussians, organized by what the robot has to do with them. Then the networks that consume them: PointNet++ in anger, sparse convolution and MinkowskiNet, point transformers. The architectural groundwork is in L05, so this lecture is about the tradeoff, not the mechanics.
  • L07Registration and map representationsICP, its point-to-plane variant, global registration, and robust alignment, you align before you fuse. Then two ways to hold a map, side by side. Volumetric: KinectFusion to Voxblox, TSDF integration and weighting, ESDFs and why the planner wants distance rather than occupancy. Neural: NeRF, positional encoding, Instant-NGP hash grids, implicit SLAM with iMAP and NICE-SLAM. Then the comparison: drift, memory, and the cost of a map you cannot query in closed form.
  • L08Active perception GuestChoosing the next measurement rather than accepting the one you get. Next-best-view selection, Fisher information and uncertainty quantification over a radiance field, information-driven exploration, and active mapping that closes the loop with the SLAM front end. Where the sensing budget goes on a robot that cannot look everywhere.Wen Jiang
  • L09Gaussian splatting SLAM3DGS optimization and rasterization, then splatting as a live map: monocular GS-SLAM, SplaTAM, incremental construction from a moving camera, and when a per-scene optimized map is worth its cost on a real platform.
  • L10Feed-forward 3D foundation modelsDUSt3R, MASt3R, VGGT. Pointmaps as an output representation. VGGT-SLAM and streaming variants. What happens to the classical SfM pipeline, the one you built by hand in L03, when a transformer replaces it.
UNIT 2

Semantics, objects, and scene structure

Weeks 7–9 · 5 lectures

Geometry becomes structure: instances, relations, hierarchy, and a spatial memory a planner or language model can query.

  • L11Lifting 2D foundation models into 3DSAM and SAM 2, CLIP and DINOv2 features, multi-view association and fusion. Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation: OpenScene, ConceptFusion. Why 3D labels are scarce and 2D priors are the workaround.
  • L12Object-centric perception6-DoF pose estimation and model-free tracking, FoundationPose. Shape completion from partial views. Articulated and deformable objects, part-level structure, affordance.
  • L133D scene graphs, open-set and task-drivenThe scene graph as a data structure: nodes, edges, and the mesh–object–place–room hierarchy. Then ConceptGraphs, Clio, HOV-SG, OpenGraph. Task-relevance as a compression criterion. Dynamic scene graphs, change detection, multi-robot construction and bandwidth.
  • L143D scene graphs, construction GuestNodes, edges, and hierarchy from mesh to objects to places to rooms to buildings. Real-time incremental construction, and optimizing a scene graph under loop closure.Yun Chang
  • L15Spatial memory and language groundingScene graphs as LLM context. Retrieval over spatial memory, hierarchical planning on a graph, embodied question answering. What a language model can and cannot infer about space.
UNIT 3

World models and prediction

Weeks 11–13 · 4 lectures

From a static model of what is there to a predictive model of what happens next under the robot's own actions.

  • L16Latent dynamicsWhat a world model is and what it is conditioned on. PlaNet and Dreamer. Model-based RL, planning in latent space, and the compounding-error problem.
  • L174D and occupancy forecastingOccupancy networks and occupancy prediction for autonomous driving. Point-cloud forecasting, scene flow, 4D reconstruction of dynamic scenes. Where the driving and manipulation literatures diverge.
  • L18Uncertainty, failure, and evaluationCalibration, ensembles, conformal prediction, out-of-distribution detection, stale spatial memory. Then: why FVD and PSNR do not predict task success, and what decision-centric evaluation looks like.
  • L19Generative 3D and video world models GuestLearned 3D content generation. Action-conditioned and controllable video prediction. World foundation models for physical AI, and the gap between a plausible video and a usable simulator.Jun Gao
UNIT 4

Perception for action

Weeks 14–15 · 4 lectures

Closing the loop. The recurring question: what does the policy actually need from perception, and how much of the pipeline survives end-to-end learning?

  • L20VLAs and the perception–action interfaceRT-2, OpenVLA, and flow-matching policies. What representation survives inside an end-to-end model. The modular-versus-monolithic argument, taken seriously in both directions.
  • L21Navigation, exploration, and instruction followingSemantic mapping for navigation. Frontier and information-theoretic exploration. ObjectNav and vision-language navigation. Scene graphs as the planning substrate.
  • L223D-aware manipulation policies GuestMulti-view rendering as a policy input, point-cloud policies, and diffusion as an action generator. What view and geometry a manipulation policy actually needs.Ankit Goyal
  • L23Deployment, data, and consequencesSim-to-real and domain randomization. Data engines and large robot datasets. Privacy and consent for persistent 3D memory of the places people live and work.

07 · Coursework

Three labs, four seminars, and a project

Each lab produces a component the next one consumes. By late November you have built a calibrated, mapped, semantically labeled, queryable 3D stack from raw sensor data.

Each lab handout, with its point breakdown and deliverables, is released on Canvas the day the lab opens.

Starter code comes with the handout: shared utilities, contract tests, a runner per lab, and every graded function left as a stub. It is on Canvas alongside the lab.

Lab 1 · Sep 14 – Oct 18 →

From raw sensors to a map

Calibrate and time-align an RGB-D and LiDAR pair from a provided ROS 2 bag. Implement ICP and a point-to-plane variant. Integrate a TSDF volume, extract a mesh and an ESDF. Close a loop with a small factor graph and report drift before and after.

Lab 2 · Oct 7 – Oct 30 →

Representations, compared honestly

Train a sparse-convolution or point-transformer segmenter on ScanNet++. Separately fit a 3DGS scene and run a feed-forward VGGT reconstruction on the same sequence. Evaluate all three against one downstream task (collision checking or grasp sampling) rather than against PSNR.

The point: the ranking flips depending on the task. You are expected to find that out, not be told it.

Lab 3 · Oct 28 – Nov 22 →

A scene graph you can ask questions

Build an open-vocabulary 3D scene graph from a posed RGB-D sequence: SAM 2 instances, CLIP or DINOv2 features, multi-view association, node and edge construction. Then answer a set of spatial and task queries by putting the graph in an LLM's context.

Deliverable: query accuracy plus a failure analysis: which queries fail, and whether the failure is in the graph or in the language model.

Seminar · four sessions, one per unit

Reading, led by students

Every paper on the reading list is required, and each is assigned to the lecture it supports. Seventeen of those lectures carry a structured response, submitted on Canvas and due at the start of the lecture, on one designated paper: the claim, the evidence, the weakest assumption, and what you would run next. The response schedule lists all seventeen with their dates. The template has the four questions, what a weak answer looks like against a strong one, and a fully worked example. Each student leads one 15-minute paper spotlight during a seminar session, paired with a reproduction sketch: what it would actually take to rerun the headline result.

Each unit closes with a seminar on its own papers: I Sep 30 (representation and reconstruction), II Nov 2 (semantics and structure), III Nov 11 (world models), IV Dec 2 (perception for action). Three of the four sit within a week of that unit's guest lecture, so you arrive at the talk having argued about the speaker's work first.

At 30% of the grade this is the largest single component after the project. There is no exam; the seminar is where the reading is assessed, and the responses are what make the discussion work.

Research project, teams of 3–4

Pick a 3D robot perception problem, find a relevant recent paper, build on it, and demonstrate the result. Robot hardware is not required; working with 3D sensor data or in simulation is fine. Ongoing research work may be used, provided it meets the requirements.

Milestones, all briefed and submitted on Canvas. Proposal naming a target paper and an evaluation, Fri Oct 23. Checkpoint with a reproduced baseline running end to end, Fri Nov 13. Presentation during the final exam period, Dec 14–18. Final report and demonstration video due Fri Dec 18.

498 and 599. Undergraduates may submit a careful reproduction plus one well-motivated extension. Graduate students contribute a novel component (a new method, a new evaluation, or a negative result established rigorously) written in conference format with related work. Same milestones, different rubric.

08 · Policies

Course policies

Collaboration

You are encouraged to discuss lab problems with other students. Written solutions and code must be your own. Do not use code from other students or from outside sources except where an assignment explicitly permits it.

Generative AI

Use the tools at your disposal, but the work you submit must be yours. Copying the output of an automated system is the same as copying the output of a classmate.

Late work

Late submissions are accepted through the end of the course with a deduction. The goal is for everyone to turn in every assignment; if something is going wrong, contact the course staff before the deadline rather than after.

Honor code and support

All students are bound by the College of Engineering Honor Code. Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS) provides support for mental health, stress, and related concerns.

09 · Resources

Compute, data, and reference material

Compute

Lab 1 runs on CPU. Labs 2 and 3 need real GPUs; Colab will not carry a 3DGS fit or a VGGT forward pass on a long sequence. A Great Lakes allocation is provided for the course; instructions are on Canvas.

Texts

No required textbook. Szeliski, Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications is the free reference for the geometric-vision notes, which cite it by section. Dellaert and Kaess, Factor Graphs for Robot Perception is the reference for Unit 1.

Camera calibration

MathWorks, Camera Calibration is the clearest short statement of the pinhole model, and L02 follows its notation: the camera matrix P = K[R t], the entries of the intrinsic matrix, and the radial and tangential distortion coefficients. Four screens, with the figures that make the two hops obvious. Read it before L02 and again before Lab 1 Part B.

Where things live

Canvas is where every assignment lives, labs and starter code, the two diagnostic quizzes, the project brief and its milestones, and all submissions. Each opens on the date in the schedule above and not before. Piazza is for questions and discussion; grades and announcements are on Canvas.

Lecture slides are posted on this page at the start of each week. The annotated build has every derivation written out; the write-in build leaves those spaces ruled and blank, for working through in the lecture or printing to annotate. Both download from the curriculum above. Earlier weeks stay up; later weeks appear as they are reached.

Every lecture is recorded and posted to LecCap. The recordings are a supplement, not a substitute: the write-in slides only make sense alongside what gets written on them in the room.
